form.opening: Opens with a short framing survey, not a case or puzzle. The first paragraph says metaphysicians and moral philosophers treat the free will problem differently. The second paragraph defines compatibilism and incompatibilism and quotes Hume and Davidson. The thesis and main aim are stated in the second paragraph: reappraise the metaphysical case for incompatibilism and propose a compatibilist account. There is no formal roadmap. The abstract does carry a one-sentence statement of the paper's three tasks. The body ends its intro with a single bridging sentence ('To see why, consider how many metaphysicians tend to view the problem').
form.sections: Nine numbered sections plus an unnumbered, untitled introduction and a short asterisk-separated conclusion. Sections run from about 300 to 1,200 words, with the early ones (1–3) and section 6 longest. Headings are numbered and descriptive, in capitals, some of them long. Examples: 'How incompatibilists can avoid the modal transfer fallacy', 'The ideal of ultimate determination'. Two are phrased as a question or noun phrase ('Is the concept of free action fundamentally historical?', 'The deliberative point of view'). Sections rarely open by summarising themselves. They start by announcing a topic or by linking to the last point ('To see how determinism bears on freedom, let's begin with…', 'So far, we have considered…'). Several close with a sentence handing off to the next section ('we should now explore…', 'The next section clarifies…').
form.argument: Mostly argued in continuous prose. One numbered argument appears: a generic consequence argument reconstructed as premises 1–5, then lettered premises A and B and conclusion C. It is set off in the middle of section 3 and is then attacked premise by premise in following prose. A second, smaller piece of notation is a three-line lettered schema (a)–(c) illustrating a modal inference. Two italicised, labelled definitions in boxed-style indented blocks give necessary and sufficient conditions ('Compulsion of voluntary action', 'Acting freely', 'Prospective freedom'), with clauses (a)–(c) or (1)–(2). Elsewhere there is light logical and modal notation: angle-bracket law forms, 'Necessarily, if…' wide-scope phrasing, and symbols like A-ing, t, tL. The positive view is built by 'first approximation' formulations, then refined with qualifications.
form.cases: Many short cases, nearly all unlabelled and introduced inline, usually in the middle of a paragraph with 'Consider…', 'Suppose…' or 'Compare…'. A thieving banker recurs from section 1 through section 3. A courier robbed at gunpoint is paired with him in section 4 as a contrast. A machine-made duplicate in section 5 is the one extended thought experiment, and it is reused in section 7 as 'another duplication case'. Others include the Socrates syllogism (an analogy), billiard balls, a dropped pen, a shotgun marriage proposal, bulldozing a house, a horn waking a sleeper, a growling pitbull and an accident victim. Cases are drawn from ordinary life, mainly in sections 4–8. Some are also used for logical points in sections 2–3. Footnote cases (bombing Chicago, a charge-card signature, Locke's prisoner) do side work.
form.objections: No dedicated objections section, and objections are seldom raised as 'Objection:' moves. Opposing arguments are treated as the target of sections 1–3, which examine the incompatibilist consequence argument and its sources. Elsewhere a rival view is voiced in one sentence and answered at once ('Someone might accept everything said so far and still claim…'; 'Is there any way to satisfy such a thirst for ultimacy?'). Roughly three or four such moments, handled by rhetorical questions and distinctions, with a concession that some issues are left open. Section 7 answers a worry about history. The conclusion also concedes limits.
form.prior_work: Dense and woven through the text and especially the notes. Authors are cited by name and date (van Inwagen, Vihvelin, Fischer, Huemer, Sartorio, Haji, Kane, Beebee and Mele, O'Connor). Quotations are often used to display wording that 'invites' a fallacy. Disagreement is phrased with hedging courtesy: 'Nothing I've said implies that the most sophisticated incompatibilists commit…', 'I believe she could agree', 'perhaps he never claims to provide'. Credit for the author's own view is given partly to earlier self-citation ('foreshadowed in Audi 1974, explicit in Audi 1993'). Hume and Davidson frame the introduction, and Aristotle is cited briefly. Heavy use of 'Cf.' and 'See' pointers to literature, and a statement that coverage is selective. There is no survey section.
form.signposting: Moderate. Signposting is mostly local: 'Let me offer a partial explanation', 'Before dealing with…', 'Several further points are needed here. First… A second… A third…', 'This brings us to a third condition'. There is no global roadmap beyond the thesis paragraph. The conclusion recaps the work done ('This paper has described… I have distinguished… I have exposed…').
form.voice: First person singular dominates ('I want to explore', 'I take', 'I suggest', 'I believe', 'I leave them open'). First person plural is used inclusively for the reader and in general claims ('we can see', 'we should now explore'). Register is formal, analytic and measured, with occasional dry wit ('what better conversationalist could the gods have?'). Hedges are frequent: 'apparently', 'seems', 'perhaps', 'surely'. Italics are used for emphasis, and scare quotes and angle brackets mark terms and propositions.
form.notes: 35 footnotes, many of them long and substantive. They carry most of the scholarly apparatus: citations to the literature, textual quotations of opponents, and qualifications. Some are extended side arguments (the asymptotic-causation caveat, the agent-causation remark, Huemer's formulation, the obligation-closure point, the Frankfurt cases). Others give self-citations and the acknowledgments (note 35, a long thank-you list). Several mark topics set aside 'to save space'.
form.ending: A short closing passage, set off by a row of asterisks inside section 9 rather than headed 'Conclusion'. It runs about 900 words. It first summarises the two approaches and the distinction drawn between two conceptions of determinism, then restates the diagnostic claim about modal idioms. It then widens: it asks whether there is one free will problem, and says more remains to be said. It admits discomfort with every position and links the view to the agent-causal tradition. It ends on a deliberate concession ('not that [incompatibilism] is false but rather that it is far from compelling'), a modest hope, and a call for further dialogue between compatibilists and incompatibilists.
form.distinctive: The paper is built as a diagnosis followed by a construction. The first third presses a single logical point about a fallacy (called 'modal transfer') against one family of arguments, and the second part builds a positive account through successive 'first approximation' formulations. The abstract is unusually programmatic, framed as a question and a statement of tasks. The numbered argument is reconstructed by the author rather than quoted. Footnotes carry unusually heavy argumentative work, including extended side arguments. The recurring banker case links sections 1–4. Sections 5 and 7 are connected by a second thought-experiment case, introduced as a pair. Prose is generous with 'Compare:' and 'Consider' prompts. Concessions and admitted vagueness are written into the argument openly ('my purposes do not require a full-scale account'). Section headings reflect shifts of topic rather than the stages of one argument.

form.opening: Opens with a statement of the topic and a framing question (how knowledge-first relates to evidentialism), then a meta-question of why either camp should care. The first paragraph announces the question; Williamson is quoted at length as motivation. The thesis is stated in the abstract and again in the final paragraph of the introduction (about the 7th paragraph). The roadmap is a single long paragraph summarising the whole argument and its upshots, with no section-by-section signposting.
form.sections: Twelve numbered sections, with a few numbered subsections (5.1–5.3). Lengths range from half a page to about three pages; the middle sections are longest. Headings are numbered and descriptive, some naming the view or the argument (e.g. 'Agrippa Plus: ...', 'Williamson's modest foundationalism', 'Trouble for ...'). Many sections open by saying what the section does or by recalling where earlier sections left things ('This section argues that...', 'Having articulated... I now go on to...', 'We have developed... but found it wanting'). Sections 7, 10 and 11 begin with a short backward-looking recap and a forward pointer.
form.argument: Mainly prose, with the central arguments set out in a semi-formal way. Named principles are given labels in parentheses, e.g. (JUST), (¬SELF), (K→J), (EVI), (E=K), set off as indented blocks. The core arguments are written out in prose as step-by-step derivations and then compressed into a named entailment schema ('Agrippa', 'Agrippa Plus', 'Agrippa Plus (partial justification)') using ∧ and ⊧. There are no numbered P1/P2/C lists. Position options are listed as (a)–(c) combinations of the premises. Formal notation is propositional-logic style only.
form.cases: Few, mostly brief, and used as illustrations rather than as the engine of the paper. There are named cases: Brutely Justified Evidence (a stipulated view), the Bad and Good conditions for a sheep-like dog, and Chisholm's dog/sheep case, which is borrowed. There are also recurring labelled subjects S1, S2, S3 in a tomato series, a calculator pair S/S*, and a wishful-thinker S*. Some are labelled and set off in indented blocks; others are told inline. They are concentrated in the second half (Sections 9 and 11), introduced with 'Consider...' or 'Imagine...'. The earlier sections use only a small illustration (wet grass).
form.objections: There is no separate objections section. Objections are raised against positions the author considers, largely in Sections 6 and 9, which are devoted to critiquing Williamson's reading and the author's own developed view. Within sections, anticipated replies are introduced with 'It could be replied...', 'The view may be saved by...', and are answered immediately, often with the charge of being ad hoc. A single list of two principal 'sources of trouble' is numbered (i)–(ii) in Section 9. The objections are mostly aimed at the view being explored, not at the author's own thesis, and the conclusion concedes the non-conclusiveness of the case.
form.prior_work: Woven through the text rather than surveyed. Feldman and Conee, Williamson, Whitcomb, Brueckner, Davidson, Kornblith, Sutton and others are named in the running text and in footnotes. Long block quotations of Williamson (and Whitcomb) are used as textual evidence and then interpreted, with alternative readings weighed. Credit and disagreement are phrased mildly ('Williamson does seem to flirt with...', 'I take my formulation from Beddor, slightly simplified'). Unpublished work and personal communication are cited. Pointers to other discussions are given in notes.
form.signposting: Heavy. The introduction gives a full preview of the results. Sections announce their aim, say what has been shown, and refer forward and back by section number ('I return to that question in Sections 6 and 7', 'we shall return to this in a later section'). There are frequent 'In summary', 'So, to conclude' and 'In short' markers even within sections.
form.voice: First person singular for the author's moves ('I argue', 'I shall', 'I conclude'), with frequent inclusive 'we' for the joint reasoning. Register is plain, analytic and lightly conversational, with a marriage/partners metaphor in the introduction and conclusion and phrases such as 'bite the bullet', 'card-carrying'.
form.notes: About 28 footnotes (footnote numbering has a small glitch around 11–13). They give citations and pointers to further reading, clarify formulations (e.g. which evidentialist formulation is used), add caveats and concessions, record personal communication and a referee acknowledgement, and make forward references to other sections. Several are fairly long.
form.ending: A conclusion of about one and a half pages. It restates the setup (each view supplies what the other lacks) and recaps the argument and its results, then the problems for the developed view, and then the lessons for the evidentialist and for the knowledge-firster. It concedes that the case against the developed view is not a knock-down refutation. It returns to the opening question about internalism versus externalism and closes with a short diagnostic remark and a historical aside (Goldman). It points to no explicit further work. Acknowledgements follow.
form.distinctive: The argument is built around a named, reusable schema ('Agrippa' → 'Agrippa Plus'), whose variants are reused throughout as a fixed point of reference. The paper is organised as an elimination of options: a trilemma-style set of positions (a)–(c) is laid out, and each is then developed or dismissed in turn. The announced aim is partly negative (the combination fails) but the paper stresses the lessons learned along the way, with sections devoted to what each camp can take from the failure. Abbreviations in capitals for positions (EKFJ) and for premises are used densely. Section 5 works as a clarificatory interlude of three subsections before the argument resumes. Clear divisions of labour are marked between establishing, exploring, criticising and drawing lessons.

form.opening: Opens with a quoted characterisation by a prior philosopher (Winch, glossed by Phillips) of what philosophy does, then moves to the programme under discussion. No case or puzzle. The overall thesis comes in the last paragraph of the Introduction (paragraph 6 of 6), after a broad framing and definitional paragraphs, though the abstract states it earlier. The roadmap is a single prose paragraph of about 200 words. It names the focal thinker, the critic, and the two-part stance (defend in principle, qualify on specific concepts). It gives no section numbers.
form.sections: Seven numbered sections with descriptive headings (e.g. 'Advocating conceptual decolonization', 'Defending Wiredu's proposal', 'Recovering religious concepts', 'Concluding remarks'). Several headings name the section's job with a gerund. They are of uneven length, roughly 600 to 2,500 words, and the body is about 7,500 words. Sections usually do not open with a recap. Instead, the closing paragraph of one section often points ahead to the next and back to earlier ones ('analysis will occur in §6'; 'The next section, then, revisits…'). Section 6 does open by setting up a framing from other authors before turning to its target.
form.argument: Entirely in continuous prose. There are no numbered premises, no formal notation, and no displayed arguments. The argument is built by exposition, then quotation, then evaluative comment. Moves are marked by connectives ('Admittedly', 'Once again it should be emphasized', 'Even so'). Critical points are phrased as rhetorical questions ('Why, however, should we assume…?').
form.cases: No invented thought-experiments and no labelled cases. 'Cases' are illustrations drawn from the literature: a handful of religious concepts treated in Wiredu, a language-and-writing example from Táíwò's discussion, one empirical research study, and a set of everyday English idioms. Authors' own examples are woven into the exposition and introduced with 'for example', 'a further example is', or 'as an exemplary case'. The expository examples sit in §3 and the critical re-examination of them in §6; neither is named or numbered.
form.objections: The objections come in a dedicated section (§4, three numbered-in-prose criticisms: 'An initial…', 'A second…', 'The third…'). The following section (§5) answers them in the same order, each opened by 'In response to the first criticism…', 'The second…', 'As for the third…'. A separate critical objection (to the focal author's own treatment) is the argument of §6. Replies are concessive: each criticism is granted as 'well taken' but held not to be decisive. Short anticipatory qualifications are also folded into the exposition. Of the main objections, about three are answered and one is raised by the author.
form.prior_work: The paper is almost entirely a critical engagement with other authors, woven through every section. §2 is a quasi-survey of advocates and rival taxonomies. Extended paraphrase with short direct quotation and in-text author-date citation dominates; the quotations carry the argument. Disagreement is phrased politely but plainly ('disappointingly shallow', 'hardly does justice', 'well taken', 'open to question'). Credit is given generously, and the author often declines to endorse or oppugn a third party's conclusions ('My reason for mentioning… is neither to endorse nor to oppugn'). Notes are used for further references and short qualifications.
form.signposting: Moderate to heavy. There is an extended roadmap, cross-references by section number ('§4 below', 'in §3 above'), and frequent self-descriptions of purpose ('My purpose in this section is…', 'What I hope to have done in this section is…', 'My purpose in outlining these examples has been…'). Closing paragraphs of sections state what was shown and what comes next.
form.voice: First person singular, used sparingly and mainly for stating aims and stances ('I argue', 'I shall', 'I concur'). Occasional inclusive 'we' ('we saw earlier', 'we might view'). The register is formal academic, with an elevated lexicon, long sentences, and a measured, even-handed tone.
form.notes: About 13 footnotes. They give clusters of supporting references, add parallel quotations, and add qualifications and asides (a correction of a quoted claim, a link to experimental philosophy, a dictionary gloss). One closing note carries the dedication and acknowledgements (to a deceased philosopher, a research group, editors and referees). Footnotes are generally short and none develops a separate argument.
form.ending: A one-section 'Concluding remarks' of about 450 words in two paragraphs. The first paragraph summarises the article's verdict and concedes the force of the critic's points. The second restates the qualified defence, recaps the example discussed, and ends by looking forward ('will require keener attentiveness…'). It gives no list of further work beyond a brief gesture in the previous section.
form.distinctive: A critical-exegetical paper organised around a figure and a critic rather than a self-standing thesis. The structure is expound, object, reply, then qualify, with the author's own contribution deferred to the penultimate section. The drawn-out exposition of the focal thinker's views (§§2–3) precedes any evaluation. A Wittgensteinian frame is brought in only at the start of §6, and the opening quotation is echoed in the title. Reconstruction is hedged ('probably', 'would probably endorse') and criticisms are stated as modest corrections rather than refutations. Long quotations are woven into sentences, and the abstract is a single paragraph that names the main figures.

form.opening: Begins with a short abstract, then Section 1 opens by describing the physics background and defining the terms BBU, BB and OO in the first two paragraphs, with a long footnote on terminology. The challenge is built up over about eight paragraphs and is then set out as a two-step skeptical argument. The thesis, a simpler Bayesian response, is first stated in the paragraph beginning 'Regardless of the merits…' near the end of Section 1, around page 3. There is no formal roadmap, only scattered forward references such as 'we will discuss Wallace below' and 'later in section 3'.
form.sections: Four numbered sections plus two appendices and a bibliography. Section 1 is about 3 pages, Section 2 about 10, Section 3 about 13 and Section 4 about 2. Headings are numbered and descriptive; the first is a question and later ones are statements. Subsections carry lettered descriptive titles such as 'Theory #1…' and 'First Explanation…'. Section 3's subsection c is a continuation titled 'Second Explanation, Continued'. Sections do open by orienting the reader, for example the opening of Section 3 announces two explanations of the temptation. Section 2 closes by restating the two-step argument and saying which step fails.
form.argument: Mostly prose, with heavy use of Bayesian notation. Displayed equations give posterior = prior × Bayes factor, and the same equation is repeated for each theory of evidence. The two-step skeptical argument is displayed as indented 'Step 1/Step 2' and repeated verbatim later with a small amendment. Numbered premises (1)–(3) appear once, in 3a. A displayed Lemma, a Defeat assumption and labelled Results 1, 2, 2.1 and 2.2 are given in Section 3b. Two formal proofs of Results 1 and 2 are in the appendices, as numbered lines with justifications in brackets. Footnotes carry side proofs and algebra. Probabilities are written Pr(X|Y), and illustrative numbers are used.
form.cases: Few narrative cases. There is a recurring apple-falling-and-rotting experience, a coffee experience, a three-marble urn case (credited to John Pittard) and a roulette wheel in a footnote. Kotzen's 'ticker tape' case and Hirsch's brain emporium case are mentioned late in the conclusion. The urn case is introduced mid-section as a supporting argument, with full set-up and a worked number. None of the cases has a formal label or name beyond a description.
form.objections: There is no separate objections section. Objections are woven into the argument, often via a rhetorical question or 'one might argue' ('Should we now be worried about…?'), and answered immediately. A footnote carries one anticipated objection, with a promise to answer it later. The 'no reason to suppose' worry gets its own explicit defusing paragraph. Several others are handled in passing, so the count is around five. The longest sustained opposition is to a rival view, Center Indifference, which takes up most of Section 3. The paper presents that as a diagnosis of why the skeptical argument tempts us, not as an objection.
form.prior_work: Woven through the text and notes, with no survey section. The positions of Carroll and Dogramaci are placed against the authors' own in Section 1. Critics of the 'instability' idea are listed in a footnote. Wallace and Builes are discussed in detail in Section 3b, with a brief exposition followed by two stated limitations of Wallace's proof. Other citations appear in footnotes as 'See X for…'. Credit is explicit ('inspired some of our own thinking', 'we thank John Pittard', 'compelling critiques'). Disagreement is stated openly but politely ('we take sides with Dogramaci and not Carroll'). The authors' own earlier work is credited with an additional explanation.
form.signposting: Heavy. The paper frequently says what it has argued and what it will do next ('What we will argue now is…', 'First…Second…'). It reminds the reader of its concessions and of the central point, which it calls 'the important thing' and 'a point we'll keep returning to'. It also points forward and back to numbered sections, results and footnotes, and re-states the two-step argument.
form.voice: First person plural throughout ('we'), with occasional 'I' and 'you' for the Bayesian reasoner in the first-person examples. The register is conversational and plain ('zillions', 'bazillion', 'freaky events', 'roll of the dice', 'good news for everyone'), with italics and exclamation marks for emphasis, and some wry humour.
form.notes: About 40 footnotes, some of them long (page-length on pages 17 and 26). They give citations with page numbers, terminological remarks, qualifications and objections, side examples, short derivations and credit. They also hold the argument for premise 2 (via (3)) and a scope remark on Wallace's title.
form.ending: The final section, about 1.5 pages, is titled 'Conclusion: the Empirical Case for Skepticism'. It reframes the paper as a message to two audiences, epistemologists and cosmologists. It concedes that some empirical evidence could support skepticism, as Kotzen's case shows. It extends the point to simulation arguments, leaves the likelihoods for those cases to others, and ends on the punchy line of the title, 'That is why I'm not a Boltzmann Brain', with an acknowledgements footnote.
form.distinctive: The title is first-personal and echoes a famous essay. It uses a 'whichever way you go' dilemma: if the contested principle is true, one conclusion holds, and if false, another. It states early what is conceded to the opponent and returns to that concession repeatedly. The proofs go in appendices while the body gives only intuitive summaries of the Results. It keeps fixed vocabulary and abbreviations (BB, OO, BBU, CI, E, HE). It diagnoses error sources, as 'explanations of temptation', after giving the positive argument. The document shows version-history notes.

form.opening: Begins with a short abstract that lists four theses, then a one-paragraph scene-setter with two example questions ('Who is the Pope?', 'How will the universe end?'). The introduction then sketches a rival account and its two core principles, and notes recent criticism of it. The thesis (defending a new account) is stated in the fourth paragraph of the introduction ('My aim in this paper is to provide a new conception...'), after the rival view has been set up. The roadmap is a short paragraph at the end of the introduction (about 4 sentences), which gives one sentence per later section with section-number cross-references. The introduction runs about 1.5 pages.
form.sections: Seven numbered sections. Section 2 has three numbered subsections (2.1–2.3) and Section 5 has four (5.1–5.4). Sections 3 and 4 are short (about 0.5 and 3 pages); 5 is the longest (about 8 pages); 6 is about 1.5 pages; the conclusion is a single paragraph. Headings are short and descriptive, with numbers ('The start of inquiry', 'Ignorance norms'). Subsection headings are in italics and sometimes playful ('Long live the ignorance norm(s)!', 'Futile intending'). Section 2 opens with a roadmap sentence listing its subsections. Sections 5 and 6 open by recalling an earlier-stated principle ('To start with, recall:', 'Recall Zetetic Instrumental Principle'). Sections close with a one-sentence hand-off to the next ('I turn now to…'). Section 2.3 and Section 5.3 each end with a brief wrap-up.
form.argument: Almost entirely in prose. There are no numbered premises or conclusions and no formal notation beyond a question-superscript and p^Q. The main theoretical principles are set off as indented, italic-named, display-quoted principles with labelled abbreviations (Exhaustivity, Sufficiency, DBI, ZIP, Intention-Exhaustivity, Intention-Sufficiency, Intention Ignorance-Norm/-Belief/-Knowledge, Take a Means). There are about 12 of these, mostly in the 'Rationality requires that (if…, then…)' schema. Two numbered example utterances appear in Section 5. The argument is carried by informal moves such as 'From this general condition… it's a rather small step to…' and 'If we think Take a Means is plausible, then so is ZIP'.
form.cases: About eight cases or illustrations. Four are named, set-off italic vignettes with sources (Kidney, Lupo, Locked Door, Change In View), grouped in one block in Section 5 and adapted from others' work; they are introduced as 'criticism… in a variety of cases. For example:'. Others are short, unlabelled and woven into the prose: the disenchanted scientist, Detective Morse (named from an earlier paper), the daydreamer versus the particle physicist, the physicist at lunch, the newly sworn-in president, and the supermarket intention. Everyday examples come in the early, expository sections. Challenge cases come once the main argument is under way. The cases are later re-used by name in Sections 5.2 and 5.4. Cases are treated as a source of data and objections, not as the starting point of the paper.
form.objections: Objections are handled inside the sections where they arise, with no separate objections section. About 6–8 in total. They are introduced by 'Perhaps, however…', 'We might worry, however, that…', 'Still, this thought may be subject to a challenge…', 'Is this overly intellectualized? Not necessarily.' (footnote form), and 'Does the Intention Account sacrifice…? Certainly not.' Rhetorical questions are common. Replies follow immediately and are often framed as 'First… Second…', or 'Fortunately, the Intention Account can respond'. Section 5 is built around a counterexample-and-reply structure: the rival view's problems are presented, a defender's strategy is shown to fail, and then the author's own reply is given. Some replies concede part of the objection ('excusable breakdowns', 'not every case…').
form.prior_work: Woven through the text with author-year citations, with no standalone literature-review section. The introduction frames the paper against one 'prominent' view and its critics, with citations bunched in parentheses. Credit and disagreement are phrased mildly: 'as Elise Woodard convincingly argues', 'pace Smith', 'recent criticisms… what they get right'. Rivals are described as 'competitors' and the paper claims to 'acknowledge' what critics get right while 'defending the spirit' of the norms. The author's own earlier work (and a closely related author's) is cited often. Foundational work (Bratman, Vendler, Hamblin) is cited in passing for background. Footnotes carry side-citations and deferrals ('adapted from…').
form.signposting: Heavy. The abstract enumerates four theses, and the introduction gives a section-by-section roadmap. Section 2 announces its subsections. Nearly every section ends with 'I turn now to…' and opens with 'Recall…'. There are frequent mid-section promises ('I'll offer some reason to accept both…', 'I raise a challenge… below'), and a mid-paper recap at the end of Section 2 ('We started with… moved to…').
form.voice: First-person singular for argumentative moves and commitments ('I claim', 'I turn now', 'I take it'), mixed with inclusive 'we' for shared reasoning ('we should embrace', 'we can understand') and occasional 'you'. The register is plain, brisk and conversational for analytic philosophy, with idioms ('Even inquirers must nap', 'Goldilocks position', 'a feature of the account and not a bug', 'jogging in place', 'rationally kosher') and some rhetorical questions.
form.notes: 26 footnotes, in the notes and acknowledgments style of a journal article. They do several jobs: cross-references to other sections, extra citations, source attributions for adapted cases, side-objections and replies (e.g. whether intentions are propositional, whether the account is over-intellectualized), concessions and refinements prompted by referees, and thanks to 'editors' or 'an anonymous reviewer' for specific clarifications. Some run to a short paragraph (notes 6, 9, 21). Note 26, attached to the final sentence, is the acknowledgments.
form.ending: A very short one-paragraph conclusion (about 5 sentences, under 100 words). It restates the thesis in one sentence, lists the four payoffs matching the roadmap, and points to 'promising ground for further inquiry'. It ends with a light pun that picks up the paper's central notion ('I hope to have convinced the reader to intend to explore it'). It makes no new concessions and does not discuss limitations.
form.distinctive: (1) The paper is built as a response to a rival view's problems. It sets out the rival's principles, shows that the new account meets each challenge, and has a section per challenge, so its structure mirrors the rival's four weaknesses. (2) Principles are named, abbreviated and re-quoted at the start of later sections, and a parallel set of 'Intention'-prefixed principles shadows the rival's, which makes the comparison easy to follow. (3) The text is largely free of heavy formal apparatus and relies on analogies from everyday planning. (4) The paper acknowledges alternative readers up front ('those attracted to a broad-tent approach… those worried about…'), a dual-audience technique that makes the claim conditional. (5) The reply to the defenders' own strategy (re-description) is staged as a failed attempt before the author's solution. (6) Quoted principles are cited with page numbers to the author's earlier work. (7) Section 2 develops the account in three short, mostly expository subsections before any argument against rivals begins.
form.topic_label: Intentions as the basis of inquiry

form.opening: Opens with a thesis-first statement in the first paragraph of the Introduction. It notes the conventional view, says the paper will argue against it, gives a quick definitional gloss on the two rival views, and states the overall conclusion. No case or puzzle comes first. The thesis therefore appears in paragraph 1, and the abstract also states it. A roadmap follows in paragraph 2: one dense paragraph of about 200 words that walks through §2.1, §2.2, §2.3, §3 and the ending, using section-number references and phrases like 'First... Then... Next... Finally'.
form.sections: Four numbered top-level sections: 1 Introduction, 2 Relativity and Shape, 3 Persistence and the Region Argument, 4 Conclusion. Sections 2 and 3 are subdivided: 2.1 to 2.3, and 3.1 to 3.5. Headings are numbered and descriptive, sometimes named after the argument or objection ('The region argument', 'The interval objection'). Subsections run from about 400 to 2,000 words, and §2.2 is the longest. Several sections open with a short orienting paragraph: §3 gives a thesis preview and a plan, and §3.1, §3.2 and §3.3 begin with 'We already mentioned...', 'The problem of ... can be put as follows' and 'So far, so good. But...'. Sections end with short recaps, such as 'This ends our argument for (P1)'.
form.argument: Both prose and numbered form. The main argument is set out once as numbered premises and a conclusion (P1, P2, C) at the start of §2.2. Prose then motivates P2 briefly and defends P1 at length, with later back-references to '(P1)' and '(C)'. A second layer in §3.2 states four labelled, named theses in a bold-label list (Intrinsicality, Conflict, Reproduction, Reduction). §3.3 then derives a conditional from three of them in prose, and the paper names a 'modus tollens inference'. Light notation appears throughout: region symbols with subscripts, frame variables (F, F′, f1, f2), coordinate pairs, and a few definitions ('Let us say that...'). There is no formal logic apart from this.
form.cases: Several recurring, lightly named examples. The inflating basketball runs through the whole paper. A book cover, with a bookshelf frame, a train frame and an exploding generator, serves as the main case. Others are a pencil cut at 12:01, fusions of a sphere and an ellipsoid (Figure 1), and an abstract two-dimensional spacetime with coordinates (Figure 2). In the final section Bud and Lou each look at a box. Cases are introduced with 'Consider...' or 'Say that...', and are used first in the classical (Newtonian) setting, then relativistically. Cases are often modified in steps (remove the occupants, make the objects momentary). The paper states its reasons for ordering the examples (material objects first, then regions). A flip-book analogy is used. Examples are mostly unlabelled by name, with some exceptions such as 'the basketball example' and 'the pencil example'.
form.objections: One objection gets its own named subsection (§2.3, 'The interval objection'), and it is set out as 'a possible objection', 'The reader might be thinking...'. It is divided into two approaches, attributed to Balashov and Cutter, each answered in turn with 'As tempting as these approaches seem...'. Other objections are handled inside sections. They include the 'natural response' that there is no fusion, which is answered with a modified case. They also include a pause before the objection to flag three points, and a set of endurantist replies treated as options. Footnotes carry further minor objections and replies, such as the 'distance' proposal and the pictorial-representation worry. About 3 to 5 objections in all, mostly anticipated rather than attributed.
form.prior_work: Woven through, with no survey section. Chalmers is the foil in §2.1, and Cutter, Balashov, Saad, Epstein and Eddon are engaged by name and page. Disagreement is phrased directly and politely: 'no one seems to have noticed', 'This point has been missed by other scholars as well', 'Contrary to what Cutter says', 'we agree with Eddon', and 'we do not believe that...'. Credit is given with 'championed by', 'defended by' and 'introduces this option on behalf of the endurantist'. Background reading and survey-style citation lists sit in the notes (footnotes 1, 2, 17 and 19). Endurantist positions are attributed in a brisk catalogue of views, each tied to a specific author and page.
form.signposting: Heavy. There is a roadmap paragraph in the introduction. Each of §3 and its subsections ends or begins with a plan or a pointer ('The plan for this section goes as follows'; 'So goes the endurantist options in a classical setting. Now for...'). There are frequent forward and backward cross-references by section number ('as we will see in §3.5', 'we noted in §2.2'), and meta-commentary on why the argument is ordered as it is. The conclusion restates the paper's 'two major goals'.
form.voice: First person plural ('we will argue', 'we find this premise hard to resist'), with occasional second-person or imperative moves ('Consider...', 'just think of...'). The register is plain and expository for analytic metaphysics, with a few informal touches ('So far, so good', 'flies in the face', 'under the hood', 'unfazed').
form.notes: About 27 footnotes, which is heavy for the length. They do several jobs: citation lists; short clarifications or hedges ('Not at the fundamental level, anyhow'); technical asides on the physics; side objections with replies (fn. 10 is a long one); scope exclusions ('for reasons of space we will omit it'); and disagreement with named authors (fns. 5, 16, 26). A few notes contain extra argument. A short acknowledgements section is followed by the references.
form.ending: A short conclusion of two paragraphs, about 400 words in total. The first paragraph summarises, as 'two major goals'. The second extends the results to a neighbouring debate, 'Edenic' shapes, using a short Bud and Lou case. It then ends with a one-sentence pointer to future work. The ending adds no concession and no objections.
form.distinctive: The paper pairs one explicitly numbered argument with a second layer of named principles that later work as hooks for the endurantist replies. It tests a claim by moving it from regions to material objects to length and back, with the reasons for this given in advance. It uses a recurring example that is progressively modified, and it flags the limits of its claims ('we do not intend to take any stance on which endurantist option is most plausible'). The Introduction compresses the thesis into one statement of the conditional result. The paper gives a theoretically balanced treatment of options in the second half in the style of a catalogue, set out classically first and then relativistically. A short abstract and a list of keywords come first.

form.opening: Opens with a second-person scene of everyday fidgeting (dentist's office, traffic, bus stop), then turns in the second paragraph to the claim that these cases matter to a dominant view. The paper's stance ('But I am sceptical') comes in paragraph 4. The thesis is a deliberately limited one: undermine the existing arguments rather than deny the phenomenon. A roadmap follows immediately in the same paragraph, about 150 words, running section by section (Sections 1–5) and ending with a statement of overall aim. The abstract also gives a four-step 'Firstly… Secondly… Thirdly… Finally' outline.
form.sections: Five numbered sections plus an unnumbered introduction. Section 1 has two numbered subsections (1.1, 1.2). Sections run roughly 2–4 journal pages each, about 3,500–4,500 words for the opening sections and shorter for later ones. Section 5 is the shortest, at about 1.5 pages. Headings are in capitals with a number, and are descriptive and topical ('The Limits of Agentive Awareness', 'A Defensive Move?'); one is a question. Subsection headings are longer, with a colon list. Sections often open by recapping the previous result and stating what this section will do ('So far, I have argued that… In this section, I will go further…'). Several end with a short summary of the position reached ('The position we have found ourselves in is this…', 'The moral is…').
form.argument: Almost entirely argued in continuous prose. There are no numbered premises or conclusions and no formal notation beyond schematic letters (φ, A–Z, D1–Dn). Key principles are set off as indented, italic-labelled, named conditions (Awareness Condition, Attention Condition, Noticing Condition), each introduced by a colon and a single-sentence statement. A dilemma is stated in prose with 'horns'. The argument advances through stipulated terminology, a rhetorical 'try it yourself' step, and conditionals ('If X were true, then…').
form.cases: A handful of short, everyday illustrative cases, and one extended scientific case. Early on come generic vignettes (drumming, jiggling change). A recurring named protagonist, 'Alice' (fiddling with her hair, drumming), is introduced in Section 2 and reused in Sections 2 and 4. There are brief one-off examples (sandwich-eating, typist, walking in a park while talking, bus hailing) introduced inline with 'Say that…' or 'For instance'. One empirical experiment (Marcel's arm-vibration study) is described in about two paragraphs with details, and later critiqued in a long footnote. Cases are mostly not labelled, apart from Alice and the coined term 'Target Occurrences' ('Targets'), which stands in for the examples throughout.
form.objections: There is no dedicated objections section. Objections are handled inside Section 4, which announces 'I want to consider two objections', and treats them one after another in the form 'The first queries… Perhaps. But…'. The second is introduced as 'The second objection I want to consider asks…'. Section 3 works through candidate rescue moves for the opponent (the Attention and Noticing Conditions) and rejects each with reasons. Section 5 treats a defensive move (Minimalism) at length, answers it ('Maybe. But…'), and then draws a dilemma-style conclusion about the opponent's options. Reviewer suggestions are also cited and answered in footnotes. Replies are generally concessive-then-rebutting, and concede that the objection could be true.
form.prior_work: The opening and Section 1 expound three named authors' arguments in sustained, quote-heavy exegesis, with page references, and carve them into positive and negative arguments. Citations are dense throughout, often as parenthetical clusters. Long lists of 'others who hold the view' sit in footnotes. Disagreements within the target camp are noted and then set aside as not needed here. Credit and disagreement are phrased with measured words ('inspired by', 'apparently contra', 'perceptive explanation', 'at best suggestive'). Opponents are called 'friends of sub-intentional actions'. Interlocutors in Section 4 are engaged by name and with technical detail, and their empirical evidence is dissected. Later work by the original proponent is used against the early arguments.
form.signposting: Heavy. There is a roadmap in the intro. Sections open by saying what they will argue and close by saying where the argument has got to. There are explicit markers ('Recall…', 'I will discuss this in Section 4', 'Needless to say', 'For now, it is sufficient to note'), forward and backward cross-references, and statements of what is being granted or set aside for the paper's purposes.
form.voice: First person singular ('I argue', 'I think', 'I want to consider') throughout, alternating with an inclusive 'we' and occasional second-person imperatives ('try out an analogous form of argument for yourself'). The register is clear and fairly conversational analytic prose, with light wit ('The argument giveth, and the argument taketh away'; 'the very scrapings of the barrel of action'; 'It keeps the letter, but nothing of the spirit') and contractions in places.
form.notes: Roughly 22 footnotes, as footnotes at the foot of the page, plus an acknowledgements note at the end. They do several jobs: long citation lists (who holds a view or who is sceptical), pointers to the debate ('for a flavour'), clarifications of terminology, side-objections from reviewers, and a long methodological critique of one experiment (footnote 16, almost a page). Some are quite substantial and carry argumentative weight. The main text stays readable without them.
form.ending: There is no separate conclusion section. The ending is the final paragraphs of Section 5, about 250–300 words. It concedes that the opponent can escape by Minimalism but argues the victory is hollow, then points to the one remaining strategy (defending a full account of intention), acknowledging that it is costly. It closes by restating the paper's modest claim ('it may have seemed fairly simple… it is in fact a rather delicate matter'). It is part concession and part pointer to future work, with only a light summary. The acknowledgements follow in a footnote.
form.distinctive: The paper is organised as an assessment of an opposing case, not as a defence of its own positive theory, and it states this limited aim at the outset. It builds its own coinages ('Targets', 'positive/negative arguments', 'the Argument from…') and conditions in italics to give structure. Section 1 reconstructs the opponents' argument and justifies treating one argument as the only negative one before any criticism starts. Section titles map onto the logical stages: reconstruction, structural fault, failed repairs, an internal tension, and the opponent's escape route. The paper tests candidate fixes in sequence ('perhaps…', 'a different tack…'), each with a named condition that is then rejected. It also uses a footnote to mark the limit of its own commitment ('not technically necessary for my purposes'). A short rhetorical wrap-up often ends a section ('The moral is…').

form.topic_label: theological fatalism, divine knowledge and the contingent a priori
form.opening: Begins with an abstract, then a short introduction that opens by defining the topic (a thesis about omniscience and free will) and posing a one-line question ('But is it true?'). The thesis is stated in the second paragraph ('I shall argue for a novel response…'). A roadmap follows immediately, as one paragraph of about six sentences walking through §§2–4 and the concluding section.
form.sections: Five numbered sections plus a references list. Section 1 is a short introduction and §2 is a medium-length exposition. §3 and §4 are the longest, and §4 has one subsection (4.1) holding several sub-arguments. §5 is short. Headings are numbered and descriptive, with the argument names built into them (e.g. 'The A Priori Belief Argument against free will'). Sections generally open by recalling what the previous argument did and saying how the new one relates to it. §4 opens with an explicit statement of its purpose ('The purpose of this section is to develop this further argument'). §3 ends with a 'To sum up' paragraph.
form.argument: Both prose and numbered premises. Each main argument is given as a short numbered three-line argument (premise, necessity premise, conclusion) set off from the text. Numbering is continuous across the paper, from (1) to (23), with lettered sub-steps such as (1a)–(1d) and (10a)–(10b) for ancillary arguments supporting premises. Five parallel arguments of the same shape appear: Master, A Priori Belief, A Priori Knowledge, Truth-Values, Set-Theoretic, plus a plural variant sketched in prose. Each is named and then defended premise by premise in the prose that follows. Formal modal notation is used: @, ◻, ⊃, with named principles (Closure, Act, Act Lemma, Belief Lemma, Knowledge Lemma, KL*, KL**). A short step-by-step derivation (4)–(9) appears in the body, justifying lemmas by necessitation, K and modus ponens. A closure principle, Closure, is stated in schematic form.
form.cases: Few narrative cases, used as brief illustrations inside the prose rather than as labelled cases. Examples include raising your hand at t (the running example), eating khinkali tonight, the manager of Manchester City, the Ukraine war tautology, an asteroid hitting Mars, and Halley's Comet (in a note). The recurring example is introduced in §2 and reused throughout. Everyday examples are introduced casually ('For instance…'). The stipulated name 'George' is used as a device in three naming arguments, each given a short name.
form.objections: Mostly woven into the sections rather than gathered in an objection section. Typical forms: 'One could object…' or 'It would be tempting to…, but this temptation should be resisted', followed by a reply in the same paragraph or the next. About 8–10 in total. Examples include the 'actually' operator, the soft-fact response, the Grim result on the set of all truths, non-rigid set membership, and nominalism about numbers. Some are answered fully and some conceded partly ('perhaps more controversial'). §5 then surveys, in compact paragraphs, the alternative responses (Ockhamism, open theism, rejecting Closure) and argues that rejecting Closure is the best. Notes carry further objections and replies.
form.prior_work: Woven through the text with name-year citations, with many literature lists in notes. §2 reviews the standard debate for about three pages: Pike's argument, then the open theist, restricted-omniscience and Ockhamist responses, each presented as a labelled position with its proponents. Credit is generous ('helpfully describes', 'seminal works of'). Disagreement is mild and mostly set aside ('I cannot do justice to…', 'not my intention to consider them all here'). There are also positioning remarks about a similar strategy in Zagzebski, and a sympathetic nod to Hunt. A long reference list follows (about 90 items).
form.signposting: Moderate to heavy. The abstract and introduction give a roadmap. The text frequently says what an argument does and how it is structured ('I call this…', 'Now that Belief Lemma is established…', 'In what follows I will present…'). The structure is made explicit through recapitulation after each argument, including a 'To sum up' and a section on 'Closing remarks'.
form.voice: First person singular ('I shall argue', 'I believe', 'I submit'), with the occasional inclusive 'we' and a generic 'you' in the examples. The register is formal analytic prose, restrained and fairly plain, with an occasional light personal touch (the khinkali example).
form.notes: 32 footnotes, some of them very long. They do several jobs: bibliographic lists of proponents; scope disclaimers ('Because of space constraints, I shall not defend it here'); technical side-arguments (a variant argument (13*)–(15*) in note 20; the Bec principle in note 31); further objections and replies; and a longer discussion of a rival fixity-of-the-past argument. The final footnote holds the acknowledgements and funding.
form.ending: A short closing section, about two pages, titled 'Closing remarks'. It summarises the lessons for restricted omniscience, then states the puzzle of what is wrong with the knowledge argument. It then runs through the options (rejecting Ockhamism, open theism, rejecting Closure) and argues for the last, listing three theoretical costs or lack thereof, with some concessions about the controversial status of claims. It ends abruptly on a statement that a controversial view is not assumed ('Of course, no such thing is assumed here'), with no grand summary.
form.distinctive: The paper is built as a series of parallel numbered arguments, each a variant of one template, and each given a name and then defended. The lemmas are proved in a short logic derivation in the body text. The author names principles in italics and refers back to them by name, which lets the later arguments be short. The first argument is a restatement of a standard one, and later arguments extend it from divine to human knowledge. Citations are heavy, in clustered lists in notes. The conclusion uses a style of weighing options rather than repeating the thesis. Each response to the later arguments is dismissed or accepted in a line or two, and many scope-limiting remarks ('not my intention to consider them all') keep the argument moving.

form.opening: Opens with a short framing statement about the influence of Frankfurt-style cases, then a named, block-indented example case (Frankfurt Action). Next it sets out a two-camp disagreement, says why settling it matters, and notes that both camps make plausible points. The thesis is first stated in the fifth paragraph of the introduction ("My proposal is..."), though the abstract has already stated it. A one-paragraph roadmap follows immediately, in order ("I will first argue... Next... I will then turn to... To conclude..."), about 120 words.
form.sections: Seven numbered sections with ALL-CAPS descriptive headings (Introduction; Preemption in Frankfurt-style action cases; ...ordinary omission cases; ...apparent Frankfurt-style omission cases; Advantages of the preemption analysis over rival analyses; A moral asymmetry...; Conclusion). Lengths are uneven: the intro and sections 2, 3 and 6 run about 1–2 pages each, section 4 about 3.5 pages, section 5 about 4.5 pages. Sections do not open with summaries of their own argument. They open with a brief orienting move: clarifications, "Before jumping into...", "We can now use Asymmetry to...", "We are now well-positioned to revisit the debate from the introduction", "Returning to the discussion from the introduction". Some close with a one-line summary or a forward pointer.
form.argument: Almost entirely argument in prose. There are no numbered premises and no formal notation. Key claims are crystallised as named, indented, bolded principles (Asymmetry; Moral Asymmetry). Reasoning proceeds by analogy between cases, by identifying causal structure, by generalising from a pair of cases, and by inference to a conclusion marked with "Hence/Thus". The paper uses inline enumerations such as "(1)... (2)", "First... Second...", and runs of ordinal replies (First through Sixth).
form.cases: About ten named cases, each in bold and set as an indented block: Frankfurt Action, Late and Early Preempting Rock, Poacher, Marathon, Stamps 1 and 2, Catapult, Potential Frankfurt Omission, No Nukes. The first is in the introduction. The rest come in the body, introduced by phrases like "Here is a standard example", "Consider the following pair", "For contrast, consider". Cases come in contrasting pairs or minimal variations with the timing changed. Each is followed by a short prose analysis, and later text refers back to the cases by name. One case is re-copied for convenience. A final case is modified step by step into the target structure. Cases are also constructed to be paradigm cases, and the author calls the omission case "the best possible candidate".
form.objections: Objections sit inside section 4 as a run of six numbered clarifications/objections ("First... Second... Third... Fourth... Fifth... Sixth, what if..."). Each is posed as a question or worry and answered with "In reply" or "In response", usually in a paragraph. One is credited to a reviewer in a note. The longer rivals are handled in a separate section, 5, covering four named rival views, each presented, then criticised, then contrasted with the author's view on simplicity and unification. A further challenge in section 6 (Cyr) is answered with three numbered points. Overall, roughly ten responses.
form.prior_work: Prior work is woven through the text and carried heavily by footnotes: lists of "see, e.g." citations for camps, background, and kinds of preemption. Rivals get a dedicated critical section, each with a short exposition, a few direct quotations, and a stated advantage for the author's view. Credit is given in a measured way ("seems right that...", "Frankfurt does seem right that..."), and disagreement is polite and framed as partial. The author also claims novelty explicitly ("no one else has yet argued...") and refers to their own earlier papers for further detail.
form.signposting: Heavy. There is an explicit roadmap, a running "as we saw / recall / as we will see" backward and forward cross-reference, "Now, let's...", "To summarize", frequent repetition of the thesis, and callbacks to the named cases and principles. Section transitions announce what has been shown and what comes next.
form.voice: First-person singular ("I contend", "I find it more plausible") mixed with inclusive "we/let's" for walking through analyses. The register is conversational-analytic and plain, with contractions here and there, and hedges like "what I hope is" and "as far as this author can tell".
form.notes: About 32 footnotes, mostly citation lists ("see, e.g."), plus some substantive ones. These include clarifications and caveats (e.g., background conditions, what "action" stands in for), pointers to the author's other papers, one reviewer acknowledgment, a long note listing theories that tie responsibility to causation (later cross-referenced), and brief replies to side questions. Notes are fairly short, with a few of 4–6 lines.
form.ending: A section 6 expands on the consequences, replies to a challenge from the literature, and sketches a possible hybrid view as future work, leaving it to another paper. The Conclusion is a single paragraph of about 250 words. It recaps the argument in order, restates the thesis, and closes on the italicised moral principle. It concedes nothing and adds no further work. Acknowledgments and references follow.
form.distinctive: The whole paper is built around a ladder of paired, labelled cases, with minimal variations used to isolate one factor. A key principle is generalised from the case pairs, named, and reapplied later. Section 5 has a modular structure (one rival per paragraph block, one or two stated advantages each). The author uses an explicit statement of assumptions and scope (what is not being argued, such as the existence of action cases). A single summary sentence follows each case analysis ("In short..."). There is a repeated motif of "straightforward explanation". The author builds the 'best candidate' case for the opposing view before analysing it.
form.topic_label: Frankfurt-style omission cases and causal preemption
aims of belief; truth-aim in inference
form.opening: Opens with a short narrative vignette of a named friend reasoning to a belief in under a minute, then moves within two paragraphs to the target view and a survey of quoted proponents. Thesis is stated in the second paragraph (the final sentence, 'we find an aimless heart'). The two premises and conclusion are set out in display in paragraph 3. A roadmap follows directly: about four sentences with section numbers. A further page of motivation says why it matters, then 'Let's get to that argument, then.' An epigraph from Plato's Meno precedes the introduction.
form.sections: Six numbered sections plus subsections (2.1–2.4, 3.1–3.2, 5.1–5.2), about 17 pages in all. Sections run from under a page (the conclusion, 1.5 pages) to about 4 pages (§2). Headings are numbered and descriptive, often playful or topic-naming ('The Doxastic Constraint', 'The Means-End Gap', 'This Problem Distinguished from Others', 'Re-homing the Aim at Truth'). Subsection headings are labelled by function ('Rival criteria…', 'First complaint: …', 'Second complaint: …', 'Can the means-end gap be filled?'). Sections usually open with a recap of what the previous section left behind or a question ('The previous section has left us with a test…', 'Make a distinction…'). Several end with a one-line wrap-up that points to what is left.
form.argument: The core argument is stated once as two named, small-caps premises and a named conclusion in the introduction. Each premise is later re-displayed when it is defended, and the conclusion is re-displayed at the start of §4. The names are re-used throughout as handles. Elsewhere the argument is in prose that proceeds through rhetorical questions and dilemmas. Several lettered, numbered mini-arguments (Arguments A–D) are displayed as numbered premise lists, built up in sequence as stages of a reductio-style regress. The paper uses one stipulated definition, quoted from an opponent. Notation is minimal: φ and ψ for the aim schema, and p. There is no formal logic apart from a modus ponens schema in prose.
form.cases: One running case, a named friend (Winifred) buying gin, appears in the first paragraph and returns in §3, §4 and §5, and again at the end. Many small ad hoc illustrations are used: auction bidding, a Hail Mary pass, seat belts, a gallbladder, a window shattering, chloroform drowsiness, a chipmunk, flying to Nepal, a reporter and a detective, math homework. They are introduced inline with 'Suppose…', 'Take me, for example', 'Think of…'. Only the lettered arguments are explicitly labelled. The running case is introduced before the argument and re-invoked as a test case ('We ought to have an example case on hand').
form.objections: Objections are handled inside sections rather than in a dedicated section. §2.2–2.4 take on rival criteria from named authors as a block of two 'complaints'. §3.2 considers attempts to fill the gap (three escalating 'fixes' with their regress). §4 distinguishes the problem from regress worries and anticipates the 'too counterintuitive' reader, whom it answers by a positive account in §5. Roughly five to six objections in all. They are introduced by 'It might be thought that…', 'Now, there's one more complication', or 'Watch the same thing happen again'. They are answered immediately, usually by showing the problem reappears one step back. Footnotes add minor ones, including an exception for taking states and a view on intentional action.
form.prior_work: Prior work is woven through from the first page. The introduction is a quotation-heavy survey of proponents with page-specific citations in the text. A named rival view is expounded and critiqued at length in §2.2–2.3 (two authors, quoted and paraphrased). Disagreement is expressed in a sprightly, direct voice ('sneaky bait-and-switch', 'only a distraction', 'I think his discussion is unsatisfying'). Credit is given in footnotes ('presses an objection like this, but without extending it as I do'; 'Setiya briefly presents a worry like this'). Allies and sources are given in see-also strings. Citations are in author-date format, with page numbers throughout.
form.signposting: Moderate to heavy. There is an explicit roadmap with section numbers, repeated back-references ('as we saw in §3.2', 'remember…', 'refer to §1'), and frequent explicit moves ('Now come to…', 'First… But, second…', 'Let's waste no time'). A recap of the argument's spirit comes at the start of §4. Section-to-section transitions are announced. The signposting is conversational rather than mechanical.
form.voice: First person singular ('I argue', 'I think', 'I demand'), with a frequent inclusive 'we'/'you' directed at the reader. The register is informal, witty and lively for analytic philosophy: contractions, jokes ('oops', 'such tollensing is their sacred right', 'nay'), and imperatives to the reader. It remains rigorous and precise in its definitions.
form.notes: Sixteen footnotes. They hold clarifications of terms (neutral definition of judgment), scope restrictions (full belief only; 'inference' defined), further citations and 'see also' lists, credits and contrasts with related worries, brief concessions and side-objections, and thanks to a referee. Some are 5–8 lines long. Most are short.
form.ending: A short conclusion of about two paragraphs. The first summarises the result in a sentence or two (a 'wedge' between inquiry and inference) and concedes that the result may disappoint. The second extends it: it states the author's own inclination, gestures at a positive alternative conception ('there is room only for a suggestion'), and defers to a manuscript. It closes on an aphoristic contrast ('When we aim, we make the world as we want it… we find it as it is'). A footnote credits intellectual debts.
form.distinctive: A named-premise skeleton that is stated up front and then re-used as labels throughout. Progressive, lettered displayed arguments (A→D) build a regress visually. Two parallel 'complaints' structure the critique of rivals. The ending of the introduction explains the stakes via three explananda, which are later used as a yardstick for each rival and each fix. The paper devotes a section to clarifying how its problem differs from nearby ones, and another to a positive 'rehoming' of the truth-aim so the thesis is not read as dismissing it. It opens with a short anecdote, an epigraph and an implied return to the anecdote in the final sections. The title and a recurring 'aimless heart' image recur at section ends.
